https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#auth
>  kubectl auth can-i VERB [TYPE | TYPE/NAME | NONRESOURCEURL]
> TYPE is a Kubernetes resource. Shortcuts and groups will be resolved.

### What did you expect to happen?

Document any available syntax for checking impersonation permission on core resources "groups", "users", ... without an api group

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/user-impersonation/
> To impersonate a user, user identifier (UID), group or extra fields, the impersonating user must have the ability to perform the impersonate verb on the kind of attribute being impersonated ("user", "uid", "group", etc.). > 
> ```yaml 
> apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
> kind: ClusterRole
> metadata:
> name: impersonator
> rules:
> - apiGroups: [""]
>   resources: ["users", "groups", "serviceaccounts"]

> ```

items.body:
### What happened?
                                                                                                                           
  kubectl create ingress accepts malformed trailing data in --rule.                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  For example, this malformed rule passes client-side validation:                                                          
                                                                                                                           
  foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage                                                                                  
                                                                                                                           
  The extra ,garbage causes TLS parsing to be skipped. The resulting Ingress has no spec.tls, despite the rule containing  
  tls=secret123.

  This is a client-side validation bug that can silently create an Ingress without the intended TLS configuration.         
                                                                                                                           
  ### What did you expect to happen?                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  The command should reject the rule because it does not match the documented format:                                      
                                                                                                                           
  host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]]                                                                                 
                                                                                                                           
  For example:                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                           
  rule foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage is invalid and should be in format host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]] 
                                                                                                                           
  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?                                                    
                                                                                                                           
  Run:                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                           
  $ kubectl create ingress demo \                                                                                          
      --rule='foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage' \                                                                   
      --dry-run=client \                                                                                                   
      -o yaml                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  Expected: the command rejects the malformed rule.                                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  Actual: the command accepts it and renders an Ingress with an HTTP rule but without a spec.tls entry.                    
                                                                                                                           
  The behavior was also reproduced with a focused unit test:                                                               
                                                                                                                           
  CreateIngressOptions{                                                                                                    
      Rules: []string{"foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage"},                                                          
  }.Validate()                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                           
  Validate() returns nil. Constructing the Ingress from those options produces zero TLS rules.                             
                                                                                                                           
  ### Anything else we need to know?                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  Root cause:                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  - ruleRegex is anchored at the start but not at the end.                                                                 
  - Validate() uses MatchString, so a valid prefix is sufficient.                                                          
  - buildTLSRules() only processes rules split into exactly two comma-separated fields. The trailing field makes the length
    three, so TLS is skipped.                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  Relevant code:                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L49   
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L223  
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L326  
                                                                                                                           
  Suggested fix: end-anchor the validation regex and add regression tests for trailing data.                               
                                                                                                                           
  I searched open and closed Kubernetes issues and PRs using command-, symptom-, and file-based queries and did not find an  existing matching report or open fix.                                                                                    
                                                                                                                           
  ### Kubernetes version                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                           
  Client Version: v1.36.2                                                                                                  
  Source tag commit: 24e2b02af5543d7910c2bb074c7264df5a8f0467                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  ### Cloud provider                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  Not applicable. This is a client-side kubectl parsing and validation issue; it does not require a cluster or cloud       
  provider.                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                           
  ### OS version                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  Windows, amd64                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  ### Install tools                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  Built/tested from a local Kubernetes source checkout with Go 1.26.4.

items.title: kubectl explain: add an -o skeleton output format for a copy-pasteable YAML starting point

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

items.body:
cc @kubernetes/sig-cli-feature-requests

## What would you like to be added?

A new `kubectl explain <type> -o skeleton` output format that renders a
resource's schema as a concise, editable YAML skeleton (field names with
placeholder values) instead of the verbose field-by-field prose that
`plaintext`/`plaintext-openapiv2` produce.

A companion `-o skeleton-comments` renders the same skeleton with short
inline `# ...` comments for fields that need explaining: `# required`,
`# enum: A|B|C`, `# map[string]string`, and a drill-down hint for fields
collapsed for depth (see below).

Example, `kubectl explain deployments.spec.template.spec.containers -o skeleton`:

```yaml
containers:
- name: "<required>"
  args:
  - ""
  command:
  - ""
  env: []
  envFrom: []
  image: ""
  imagePullPolicy: ""
  lifecycle: {}
  livenessProbe: {}
  ports: []
  readinessProbe: {}
  resources: {}
  securityContext: {}
  startupProbe: {}
  stdin: false
  stdinOnce: false
  terminationMessagePath: ""
  terminationMessagePolicy: ""
  tty: false
  volumeDevices: []
  volumeMounts: []
  workingDir: ""
```

Design notes:
- Placeholder values come from the schema's own `default`, else the first
  `enum` value, else `example`, else a type-appropriate zero value. A
  required field with none of those (typically a bare string) gets the
  literal `"<required>"` sentinel so it isn't mistaken for an intentionally
  empty optional field.
- The `status` subresource and server-managed `metadata` fields
  (`resourceVersion`, `uid`, `managedFields`, etc.) are omitted, since nobody
  hand-authors those.
- To keep output readable on resources with deep optional structure (Pod's
  `affinity`/`tolerations`/`securityContext`, CRD validation schemas), each
  optional field spends against a small budget before its own optional
  children collapse to a placeholder with a drill-down hint (e.g.
  `# optional, nested further -- see: kubectl explain pods.spec.affinity -o skeleton`).
  Required fields are free, so a load-bearing chain like
  `containers[].image` always expands regardless of depth.
- Implemented as one more template in the existing `pkg/explain/v2`
  template-based generator (same mechanism as `plaintext-openapiv2`), so it
  only touches the openapiv3 explain path.

## Why is this needed?

`kubectl explain` today is documentation-first: it's great for looking up
what a field means, but not for the common case of "I want to write a
Deployment/CRD manifest and need a skeleton to fill in." Today's next-best
alternatives (`kubectl create deployment ... --dry-run=client -o yaml`,
hand-copying from docs, or `explain --recursive`) either only cover a
handful of built-in kinds, produce output flooded with every field
regardless of relevance, or don't work at all for CRDs.

`-o skeleton` gives a fast, copy-pasteable starting point for any resource
the cluster serves an OpenAPI v3 schema for, including CRDs, while staying
short enough to read. The optional-depth budget means you see the fields
that actually need decisions (`containers[].image`) without also seeing
every leaf of `affinity`/`tolerations` you probably don't need today, and
you can always drill into a collapsed field with a normal
`explain <type>.<field> -o skeleton` call.

This is proposed as a proof of concept with a working implementation and
test suite already in hand (unit tests covering required/optional
ordering, enums, maps, `$ref` cycles, field-path drill-down, and the
depth-budget behavior). Happy to open the PR once there's SIG CLI agreement
on the approach/flag naming.

items.body:
### What happened?

Argo CD controller crashed when the caller lacks RBAC permission instead of erroring. https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues/28607

`kubectl auth reconcile` panics with a nil-pointer dereference when reconciling a
`RoleBinding` or `ClusterRoleBinding` if the underlying reconcile operation returns an
error (e.g. a `forbidden` response because the caller lacks RBAC permissions)

**Proposed fix**: add the same if err != nil { return err } guard after
retry.RetryOnConflict(...) in both the *rbacv1.RoleBinding and
*rbacv1.ClusterRoleBinding cases.


### What did you expect to happen?

`kubectl auth reconcile `should return the underlying error (e.g. the forbidden error)
and exit non-zero, exactly as it does for Role/ClusterRole, instead of panicking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reconcile a RoleBinding as a user without permission to get/create it:

```
cat > rb.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: test-rb
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: some-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: nobody
  namespace: default
EOF
```

kubectl auth reconcile -f rb.yaml --as=system:serviceaccount:default:nobody

Instead of a clean forbidden error, kubectl panics:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=...]

k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/auth.(*ReconcileOptions).RunReconcile.func1(...)
        .../pkg/cmd/auth/reconcile.go:274 +0x...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.(*DecoratedVisitor).Visit...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.ConcurrentVisitorList.Visit.func1()
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup.(*Group).Go.func1()
```

### Anything else we need to know?

introduced in v0.35.0 and still present on master.
v0.34.0 guards all four cases correctly; the retry.RetryOnConflict rewrite that
landed in v0.35.0 added the retry wrapper to the binding cases but omitted the
if err != nil { return err } check that the Role/ClusterRole cases retained.

Found using Argo CD impersonation feature

labels.name: kind/feature

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Improve shell completion for the `--dry-run` flag on mutating `kubectl` commands
(`apply`, `create`, `delete`, `patch`, `scale`, …) so that:

- `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>` completes to **`--dry-run=`** (with no trailing
  space and no file listing), and
- `kubectl apply --dry-run=<TAB>` suggests the valid values **`none` / `server` /
  `client`**.

**I'm working on this.** There is a cross-repo dependency: `--dry-run` carries an
optional value (it sets `NoOptDefVal` to support the deprecated bare `--dry-run`),
and cobra currently offers no way for a program to make a flag complete as
`--flag=`. I've opened an opt-in enhancement upstream in cobra to enable it:

- spf13/cobra#2433 — adds `Command.MarkFlagAppendEqual`

Once that lands and is vendored, the kubectl side is a small change in
`AddDryRunFlag` (registering value completion for `none/server/client` and
calling `MarkFlagAppendEqual("dry-run")`).

### Why is this needed?

For a flag with `NoOptDefVal` set, the only syntax that actually assigns a value
is `--dry-run=value`; `--dry-run value` (space-separated) treats `value` as a
positional argument and errors. Yet today `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>`
completes to `--dry-run ` (with a space) and then offers file completion, which:

- nudges users toward the non-working space-separated form, and
- gives no hint of the valid values (`none`, `server`, `client`).

Guiding users to `--dry-run=client` / `--dry-run=server` via completion makes the
flag more discoverable and steers them away from the deprecated bare `--dry-run`.

/sig cli
/kind feature

items.title: kubectl port-forward: no way to suppress 'Handling connection for' messages

labels.name: kind/feature

items.body:
## What happened?

`kubectl port-forward` unconditionally prints "Handling connection for <port>" to stderr on every connection.  There is no flag to suppress these messages.

For long-running tunnels with frequent connections, this produces a constant stream of noise that buries actual errors on the same file descriptor.

## What did you expect to happen?

A `--quiet` or `--verbosity` flag (or gating behind `-v` log levels) so users can suppress informational messages while preserving real errors on stderr.

## How can we reproduce it?

```
kubectl port-forward pod/any-pod 5432:5432
```

Connect to localhost:5432 from another terminal.  Each connection prints:

```
Handling connection for 5432
```

There is no way to disable this without filtering all of stderr, which risks hiding real errors.

## Anything else we need to know?

The message originates from a hardcoded `fmt.Fprintf(o.Out, "Handling connection for %d\n", port)` in `pkg/cmd/portforward/portforward.go` with no verbosity check.

Gating it behind `klog.V(1)` or similar would be sufficient.

## Environment

- kubectl version: client v1.33
- OS: macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5.0)

items.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP` writes every dump file via `setupOutputWriter`, which does:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126 (func setupOutputWriter)
file, err := os.Create(fullFile)
```

`os.Create` opens files `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` with mode `0666` before umask. With the very common `0022` umask that is `0644` (world-readable); with `0002` (common on shared systems / some distros) it is `0664` (group- and other-readable). Parents are created `0755` (`os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)` at line 124), so the directory tree is traversable by "other".

Pod logs are dumped verbatim to `{DUMP}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt` (line 295 → `writer.Write(data)` at line 287, raw bytes straight from the `log` API). Pod logs routinely contain application secrets: bearer tokens, DB connection strings, cloud credentials, signed URLs, signed certificate/key material, etc.

### What did you expect to happen?

Dump files should be created owner-only (`0600`), and the dump directory tree owner-only (`0700`) when it contains pod logs or other potentially sensitive cluster state, so that an unprivileged local user cannot read the operator's cluster dump.

Preconditions on the victim host: another local user can traverse the path to DUMP (the typical case — DUMP in a home dir, `/tmp`, a shared scratch dir, or a CI artifact dir whose parents are `0755`). The attacker needs **no Kubernetes API credentials at all** — only filesystem read on files kubectl itself just created.

1. Authorized/privileged operator runs kubectl once:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP --all-namespaces
   ```
   kubectl creates DUMP and all nested dirs `0755`, and every `logs.txt` (and `nodes.txt`, `events.txt`, …) `0644`/`0664`, with full pod-log contents — across **all** namespaces requested.
2. A second unprivileged local user reads the logs directly:
   ```bash
   cat $DUMP/*/leaky/logs.txt        # 044-mode readable + traversable parents (0755) => readable by "other"
   ```
   No exploit primitive required — ordinary filesystem ACLs. `--all-namespaces` widens the blast radius to logs from every namespace, including ones the attacker has no RBAC right to read.
3. Extract whatever secret the logs leaked (token, password, cert+key), then use it against the cluster or upstream systems:
   ```bash
   kubectl --token=<LEAKED> ...        # if a bearer token was logged
   # or use a leaked DB connection string / cloud credential against the corresponding backend
   ```
   → access beyond the attacker's normal reach, often as a high-privilege workload identity.

Exposure is **durable**: the files persist at `0644`/`0664` on disk under DUMP until someone manually tightens permissions or deletes them, and re-running the dump re-creates them the same way. On a shared host captured by automation, the window can stay open indefinitely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run this single self-contained snippet from the root of a Kubernetes checkout. It spins up a fake API server that returns one pod whose `log` endpoint serves a secret marker, then runs the real `kubectl cluster-info dump` and reports the resulting file mode + leak. It uses an already-built `kubectl` (`_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl` or `_output/bin/kubectl`).

```bash

KUBECTL="${KUBECTL:-_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl}"
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || KUBECTL=_output/bin/kubectl
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || { echo "build kubectl first: make kubectl"; exit 1; }

kubectl_bin = sys.argv[1]

def list_obj(kind, items=None):
    return {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": items or []}
def apps_list(kind):
    return {"apiVersion": "apps/v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": []}
pod = {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": "Pod",

       "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "app", "image": "busybox"}]}, "status": {"phase": "Running"}}

        if p == "/api/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "v1", "resources": []})

        if p == "/apis/apps/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "apps/v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/api/v1/nodes": return self.send_json(list_obj("NodeList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/events": return self.send_json(list_obj("EventList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/replicationcontrollers": return self.send_json(list_obj("ReplicationControllerList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/services": return self.send_json(list_obj("ServiceList"))

try:
    cmd = [kubectl_bin, f"--server=http://127.0.0.1:{port}", "--kubeconfig=/dev/null",
           "cluster-info", "dump", "--namespaces=default", "--output-directory=" + out, "-o", "json"]
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print("ERROR: kubectl cluster-info dump failed", file=sys.stderr)
        print(r.stdout, file=sys.stderr); print(r.stderr, file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(r.returncode)
    lp = pathlib.Path(out) / "default" / "leaky" / "logs.txt"
    content = lp.read_text(); mode = stat.S_IMODE(lp.stat().st_mode)
    print(f"kubectl        : {kubectl_bin}")
    print(f"dump_dir       : {out}")

The pod log containing the secret marker is written to a mode-`0664` (or `0644`) file readable by other local users. No API binding or real cluster is involved.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Sink: `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126`, `func setupOutputWriter`, called from the dump path (e.g. pod logs at line 295; also nodes/events/services/pods/etc.). Parents created `0755` at line 124.
- Same class as the already-reported client-go kubeconfig migration (`0666`→`0644`) and kubeadm/kube-scheduler config writers — sensitive runtime output written `0666` before umask instead of owner-only.

### What happened?

`kubectl apply --dry-run=client` fails for existing CRD resources with an error
"applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil". 


### What did you expect to happen?

The command should perform successful dry-run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the following script, which creates a CRD and the tries to perform
an apply with the `--dry-run=client` option:

```
#!/bin/sh
set -x -e

cat > "crd.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

cat > "crd-modified.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
  labels:
    bug-repro: "true"
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

kubectl apply -f crd.yaml

kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
```

The output:
```
+ cat
+ cat
+ kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/bugs.bug-repro.example.com created
+ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
error: error when applying patch:

to:
Resource: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Resource=customresourcedefinitions", GroupVersionKind: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Kind=CustomResourceDefinition"
Name: "bugs.bug-repro.example.com", Namespace: ""
for: "crd-modified.yaml": applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil
```


### Anything else we need to know?

**Other versions affected**

Reproduces also with kubectl 1.36.0

**An attempt at root cause analysis**

The problem is in 'k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/patcher.go':

1. PatchLocal is called for --dry-run=client. It calls patchSimple with the localApply=true. (the last argument):

``` 
func (p *Patcher) PatchLocal(current runtime.Object, modified []byte, errOut io.Writer) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
	return p.patchSimple(current, modified, "", "", errOut, true)
}
```

Below is patchSimple(). 

At lines 111 and 136 it determines whether the resource supports StrategicMergePatch using OpenAPI and OpenAPI V3 schemas and tries to produce such a patch. 

CustomResourceDefinition is one of such resource kinds, so it will create a patch and set  `patchType` to StrategicMergePatchType. 

patch!=nil, so it will not enter the block on line 149.

The applied resource differs from the current version ,so patch won't be empty,
so it will continue after the check on line 168.

localApply=true, so it will enter the block at line 171

Here on 174 it will call `scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)`, which will fail because CRD is in 'apiextensions.k8s.io/v1', apiextensions are not  builtin k8s types, so the call will fail. 

The code skips checking error status (probably it assumes (erroneously) that StrategicMerge patch always comes from line 149).

So after ignoring the error it calls `strategicpatch.StrategicMergePatch(current, patch, versionedObj)` with versionedObj==nil.

This call fails with the cryptic error "expected a struct, but received a nil" 


```

   107			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("retrieving original configuration from:\n%v\nfor: %w", obj, err)
   108		}
       
   109		var patchType types.PatchType
   110		var patch []byte
       
   111		if p.OpenAPIV3Root != nil {
   112			gvkSupported, err := p.gvkSupportsPatchOpenAPIV3(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)
   113			if err != nil {
   114				// Realistically this error logging is not needed (not present in V2),

   140				if patchType, err = p.getPatchTypeFromOpenAPI(openAPISchema, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind); err == nil && patchType == types.StrategicMergePatchType {

   145					}
   146				}
   147			}
   148		}

   152				patchType = types.StrategicMergePatchType

Bug description
kubectl cp fails on large files and leaving hanging tar zombie process inside the pod 
Scenario:
1. create a pod in k8s with attached pvc - or even with temporary file system.
2. create a large file of several GB inside the pod.
3. copy the pod from inside the pod to a target location where space is lacking.
4. the kubectl cp uses tar inside the pod and will fail due to not enough space.
5. the tar file will be hanging inside the pod .
6. file handle pointing to the file will stay 
7. If using pvc of cephfs - if somone deletes the file , the system does not see it but the cephfs has a stray file
which will never be released till the tar process will be killed or the pod will be terminating -> e.g: killing the tar file

the scenario will eventually cause a "leak" in ceph fs , and might consume all cluster data 
in case this scenario repeats it self during repeated timer

### What happened?

While trying to use `kubectl diff` on Windows, I tried to specify the absolute path to the `diff.exe` shipped with Git Bash via `KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF`. This lead to the following error message:

```
error: failed to run "C:\\Program": executable file not found in %PATH%
```

### What did you expect to happen?

`kubectl diff` should run `C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\diff.exe` when instructed to do so.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install Git on a Windows machine
2. Run the following PowerShell commands:
   ```powershell
   $env:KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF='C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\diff.exe'
   kubectl diff -f my_file.yaml
   ```

### Anything else we need to know?

As an (ugly) workaround, one can use:

```powershell
$env:KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF='C:\PROGRA~1\Git\usr\bin\diff.exe'
```

(Assuming 8.3 file names are enabled.)

Any attempts to quote the path fail as well:
```powershell
$env:KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF='"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\diff.exe"'
```
```powershell
$env:KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF="'C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\diff.exe'"

### What happened?

When migrating Appian to an on-premise RKE2 kubernetes cluster using the official Appian tool, we ran into a problem where it hangs forever. We did some troubleshooting and found the reason was because a kubectl copy command hangs when copying many files to PV. We have managed to reproduce the error using busybox and dummy files. The command finishes inside the container with exit code 0, but the kubectl session don't close. 

We reported a bug to RKE2, but they said that any of the components involved are not part of RKE2 [RKE2 issue 10237](https://github.com/rancher/rke2/issues/10237). Tried to copy files using `crictl exec` from the local node directly, which is working. We now believe it is a bug related to communication between kubectl and kube-api and possible in the kubernetes version. 

We have been able to create a work around by putting a load balancer in front and doing a rolling reboot of the manager nodes when it hangs, but when pointing the kubeconfig directly to one of the manager nodes this problem occurs.

items.body:
### What happened?

When creating a Job (e.g. `completions: 4`, `parallelism: 1`), the Job's STATUS column in `kubectl get job` shows `Running` even though all of its pods are in `Pending` state.

```console
$ kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml
job.batch/sleep-job created

$ kubectl get job
NAME        STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
sleep-job   Running   0/1 of 4      3s         3s

$ kubectl get pods
NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
sleep-job-5lp4b              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-b2kvh              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-h7pt4              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-rdnlc              0/1     Pending   0          9s
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-2dp67   1/1     Running   0          30h
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-pwfbc   1/1     Running   0          30h
```

The Job status is misleading — it reports `Running` when no pods are actually running (all are `Pending`).

### What did you expect to happen?

The Job STATUS should reflect that no pods are currently running. When all pods are in `Pending` state, the Job status should not show `Running`. A status like `Pending` or `Suspended` (or a new status that distinguishes "created but not yet scheduled") would be more accurate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job manifest with `completions: 4` where pods will remain `Pending` (e.g., due to insufficient resources, unschedulable nodes, or a simple sleep Job on a cluster with limited capacity):

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  completions: 4
  parallelism: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: sleep
        image: busybox
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```

2. Apply the manifest: `kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml`
3. Observe Job status: `kubectl get job`
4. Observe pod status: `kubectl get pods`
5. Note that the Job shows `Running` while all pods show `Pending`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This can be confusing for users debugging scheduling issues, since the Job status suggests work is actively running when it is not.

items.body:
### What happened?

When I delete a resource that has the foregroundDeletion finalizer using kubectl without any options, as shown below, 
the finalizer which is defined on the resource by server side is not honored and the deletion is performed in the background.

```
$ kubectl delete daemonset.apps/test-foreground
```

While I use a daemonset resource as an example in this issue,
this behavior is not limited to daemonset and happens for other types of resources like deployment.

I am aware that the delete subcommand provides the --cascade option. However, all available values explicitly specify the deletion propagation policy,  as shown below:

```
$ kubectl delete --cascade='background' daemonset.apps/test-foreground
```
-> Deletes dependent resources using background deletion.

```
$ kubectl delete --cascade='orphan' daemonset.apps/test-foreground
```
-> Orphans dependent resources.

```
$ kubectl delete --cascade='foreground' daemonset.apps/test-foreground
```

-> Forces foreground deletion, regardless of which finalizers are set on the resource.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected kubectl delete (without explicitly specifying --cascade) to respect the finalizers defined on the resource by server-side.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.0
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

Create the following DaemonSet with the foregroundDeletion finalizer:

```
$ cat test-deletion.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
 labels:
   app: test
 finalizers:
 - foregroundDeletion
 name: test-deletion
 namespace: default
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 600"]
        image: docker.io/busybox:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        name: test-deletion
```

Apply the manifest:

```
$ kubectl apply -f test-deletion.yaml
daemonset.apps/test-deletion created
```

Confirm that the DaemonSet and Pods are running:

```
$ kubectl get all -n default
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/test-deletion-g2mv9   1/1     Running   0          8s
pod/test-deletion-xjs5j   1/1     Running   0          8s

NAME                 TYPE        CLUSTER-IP   EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)   AGE
service/kubernetes   ClusterIP   10.96.0.1    <none>        443/TCP   8d

NAME                           DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR   AGE
daemonset.apps/test-deletion   2         2         2       2            2           <none>          8s
```

Delete the DaemonSet:

```
$ kubectl delete -v 8 -n default daemonset.apps/test-deletion
(snip)
I0306 04:42:54.953199 2157769 helper.go:202] "Request Body" body=<
        {"propagationPolicy":"Background"}
 >
I0306 04:42:54.953762 2157769 round_trippers.go:527] "Request" verb="DELETE" url="https://127.0.0.1:32861/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/daemonsets/test-deletion" headers=<
        Accept: application/json
        Content-Type: application/json
        User-Agent: kubectl/v1.35.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/6645204
 >
(snip)
daemonset.apps "test-deletion" deleted from default namespace
(snip)

```

Check the kube-controller-manager logs:

```
$ kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-kind-control-plane
```

Relevant log entries show that dependent resources are deleted with propagationPolicy="Background":

```
I0305 19:42:54.967830       1 garbagecollector.go:506] "Processing item" item="[v1/Pod, namespace: default, name: test-deletion-g2mv9, uid: 52a46707-3e67-4018-8d93-62846cdb6b7e]" virtual=false

I0305 19:42:54.968024       1 garbagecollector.go:506] "Processing item" item="[v1/Pod, namespace: default, name: test-deletion-xjs5j, uid: 85b7a176-03f7-4b0f-b3ce-6196b1a68410]" virtual=false
I0305 19:42:54.977457       1 garbagecollector.go:645] "Deleting item" item="[v1/Pod, namespace: default, name: test-deletion-g2mv9, uid: 52a46707-3e67-4018-8d93-62846cdb6b7e]" propagationPolicy="Background" 
I0305 19:42:54.977659       1 garbagecollector.go:645] "Deleting item" item="[apps/v1/ControllerRevision, namespace: default, name: test-deletion-75ffff4c44, uid: 5135a898-2a4f-45c3-a4d8-d9944817bc5c]" propagationPolicy="Background" 
I0305 19:42:54.980137       1 garbagecollector.go:645] "Deleting item" item="[v1/Pod, namespace: default, name: test-deletion-xjs5j, uid: 85b7a176-03f7-4b0f-b3ce-6196b1a68410]" propagationPolicy="Background" 
```

### Anything else we need to know?

When I delete the same resource using the Kubernetes API directly or using client-go without explicitly specifying a deletion propagation policy, 
the foregroundDeletion finalizer is respected and the deletion proceeds in the foreground as expected.
This behavior differs from kubectl delete, which appears to implicitly default to background deletion and override the resource’s finalizers.

When I deleted the same resource using these methods, the kube-controller-manager logged messages like the ones shown below.
From these logs, we can see that dependents were set between the DaemonSet and the pods before deletion, and that the deletion order was changed accordingly.

In contrast, when deleting the resource with kubectl, there were no such logs, and the foregroundDeletion finalizer appeared to be overridden.

$ kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-kind-control-plane

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

What happened?

We manage Deployments declaratively using kubectl apply (server-side apply) from GitOps pipelines.

In production, a user manually edited a Deployment (kubectl edit deployment) and added an extra environment variable directly under:
spec.template.spec.containers[].env

Later, the Deployment was redeployed using kubectl apply -f <manifest.yaml> with a manifest that does not contain this manually added env var.

Despite successful apply and no reported conflicts, the manually added environment variable remains present in the live Deployment.

This results in permanent configuration drift between the manifest and the cluster state.


### Why is this needed?

We expected the live Deployment to exactly match the applied manifest, such that:
Environment variables not present in the manifest are removed from the Deployment
kubectl apply enforces declarative state, even for mergeable lists like env
The applied manifest becomes the source of truth

In short:
After apply, the cluster state should be fully in sync with the manifest.

**How can we reproduce it**
1. create a deployment

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: sample-app
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: sample
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: sample
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: app
            image: nginx
            env:
            - name: Testing
              value: "working"
    
    kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

2. Manually edit the Deployment

    kubectl edit deployment sample-app
  
    env:
    - name: Testing2
      value: workingNot

  kubectl describe deployment sample-app

3. Re-apply the original manifest
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

4. Observe the result
kubectl describe deployment sample-app
❌ Testing2=workingNot still exists, even though it is not in the manifest.

**Anything else we need to know?**
Even tried with the below commands 
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side --force-conflicts --field-manager=gitops
Still it is not able to remove the additional env variables. 

There is currently no supported way to say:
“This list must exactly match the manifest.”
using kubectl apply

**Kubernetes version**
1.32.6

**Cloud provider**
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

## Problem

The `appProtocol` field (GA since v1.20) is not displayed in `kubectl describe service` output, even when set. Users must use `kubectl get svc -o yaml` to verify this field.

This can be problematic when debugging Service Mesh or Gateway API configurations where `appProtocol` affects traffic routing. Given that `appProtocol` has been GA for several years and is actively used in Service Mesh environments, displaying it in `kubectl describe` output would be beneficial for users.

## Proposed Solution

Display `appProtocol` in the port section of `kubectl describe service` output:
```
Port:              http  80/TCP
TargetPort:        8080/TCP
AppProtocol:       http          # <-- Add this
NodePort:          http  30080/TCP
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/describe/describe.go#L3015

## Benefits

- Consistency with other port fields (`name`, `protocol`, `port`, `targetPort`, `nodePort`)
- Easier debugging for Service Mesh and Gateway API users

labels.name: kind/documentation

items.body:
The PowerShell example in the [kubectl completion](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_completion/#examples) docs uses a plain path to the `completion.ps1` script when adding to user's profile script. This invokes the script via the [call operator](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_operators?view=powershell-7.5#call-operator-) (`&`) by default and runs in a child scope. The kubectl completion setup in the child scope is lost immediately after the script's execution and provides no benefit to the parent/user scope.

Additionally, the path to the `completion.ps1` script when written to the PowerShell profile with `Add-Content` isn’t quoted. This could raise an issue with some user's `$HOME` paths containing spaces (i.e. `C:/Users/Full Name/`), which would prevent the script from loading properly.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b067e452909f31fe3a8b018696678737ad3fc66e/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/completion/completion.go#L103-L106

```powershell
# Powershell Profile - After running Add-Content ...
C:\Users\Full Name\.kube\completion.ps1
```

When multiple StorageClasses are annotated as default (`storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`), Kubernetes uses the most recently created one as the actual default applied to PVCs without an explicit storageClassName.

```
NAME                       PROVISIONER                   RECLAIMPOLICY   AGE
nfs-client (default, effective)   k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...  Delete          3s
standard   (default, inactive)    rancher.io/local-path Delete         48m

NAME         PROVISIONER                   DEFAULT   EFFECTIVE   AGE
nfs-client   k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...           true      true        3s
standard     rancher.io/local-path         true      false       48m
```

now display
```
NAME                    PROVISIONER                RECLAIMPOLICY   AGE
nfs-client (default)    k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...        Delete          3s
standard   (default)    rancher.io/local-path      Delete          48m

### What happened?

When running `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`, some events (such as OOMKilling events from kernel-monitor node-problem-detector) do not appear, even though they are visible in `kubectl get events`. Upon investigation, these missing events have an `involvedObject` without an `apiVersion` field.

Example:

This event is **not** shown by `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`:

```yaml
kind: Event
count: 1074
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-07T22:00:52Z"
involvedObject:
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: XXXXXXXXXX
# apiVersion is missing
message: ...
reason: OOMKilling
source:
  component: kernel-monitor
```

But this event **is** shown:
```yaml
kind: Event
count: 11
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-09T01:19:49Z"
involvedObject:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: df71ea00-f008-41b2-bb6e-a21466b7bf38
# apiVersion is present
message: ...
reason: DisruptionBlocked
source:
  component: karpenter
```

The relevant code in `kubectl events` sets a field selector:
```go
listOptions.FieldSelector = fields.AndSelectors(
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.kind", o.forGVK.Kind),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.apiVersion", o.forGVK.GroupVersion().String()),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.name", o.forName)).String()
```
Events missing `involvedObject.apiVersion` are excluded from the results.

### What did you expect to happen?

Events for the specified Node should be shown even if their `involvedObject.apiVersion` field is missing, as long as `kind` and `name` match.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install node-problem-detector in the cluster
2. Generate a node event with OOMKilling (e.g., run a memory-hogging process on a node).
3. Ensure an event is created that is visible in `kubectl get events` but missing `involvedObject.apiVersion`.
4. Run `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`
5. Observe that the event does not appear, but it does with `kubectl get events`.

This bug can be worked around by omitting `--for`, but that makes filtering by object impossible. The filtering logic should be more tolerant to missing fields.

### What happened?

Running `kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0` doesn't overrides configured or default value. Pod is not visible then in `kubectl get pods` output, but container is running on the host until the grace period is over. Kubelet provides these logs.

```
Jul 31 08:16:05 ip-xyz kubelet[4405]: I0731 08:16:05.379630    4405 kubelet.go:2467] "SyncLoop DELETE" source="api" pods=["default/test2"]
Jul 31 08:16:05 ip-xyz kubelet[4405]: I0731 08:16:05.379807    4405 kuberuntime_container.go:779] "Killing container with a grace period" pod="default/test2" podUID="c0f3c430-8f01-4a61-82a8-f7fb2c528c70" containerName="test2" containerID="containerd://2ca9928cd0f3208338303e4180c057f79d86f5ae99d8a3a36965c4c835dd9ae2" gracePeriod=30
Jul 31 08:16:05 ip-xyz kubelet[4405]: I0731 08:16:05.395144    4405 kubelet.go:2461] "SyncLoop REMOVE" source="api" pods=["default/test2"]
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect CLI option --grace-period should override configured or default gracePeriod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
kubectl run test2 --image=docker.io/alpine:2.6 sleep 10000
kubectl delete pod/test2 --force=true --grace-period=0
```

And then on host where pod is running
```
ctr -n k8s.io c list | grep alpine

```bash

  kubectl create service clusterip my-svc --clusterip="None" -o yaml --dry-run=client | kubectl set selector --local -f
- 'environment=qa' -o yaml | kubectl create -f -
  kubectl create deployment my-dep -o yaml --dry-run=client | kubectl label --local -f - environment=qa -o yaml |
